case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a public official’s decision to block constituents from interacting with the official’s social-media account constitutes state action (and action under color of law) such that the First Amendment limits that moderation decision.
case_analysis.legal_provision: U.S. Const. amend. I (and incorporation via amend. XIV); 42 U.S.C. § 1983 ("under color of" state law) and the state-action doctrine.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners (school-board members) argue that blocking users from their social-media pages was not attributable to the State because the accounts were personal or mixed-use accounts not operated with governmental authority; they contend the Ninth Circuit applied an overly loose state-action standard that effectively constitutionalizes moderation decisions on officials’ private pages whenever the pages discuss public issues, and they seek a clearer, narrower test (more like the Sixth Circuit’s) under which these facts would not qualify as state action.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents (the blocked users) argue that the officials used the pages as channels for official communication and constituent engagement—posting or resharing information about school-board business and using the accounts in ways tied to their roles—so the interactive portions of the pages functioned like an official forum; blocking critics, they contend, was therefore state action/under color of law and amounted to unconstitutional viewpoint discrimination in a public forum (or at least in a forum the officials intentionally opened for discussion of official matters).
key_precedents: Lindke v. Freed (U.S. Supreme Court granted cert.; Sixth Circuit decision below discussed as applying a more stringent state-action test)
Biden v. Knight First Amendment Institute, 141 S. Ct. 1220 (2021) (vacatur; referenced for implications regarding government officials’ social-media use)
Garnier v. O’Connor-Ratcliff (Ninth Circuit decision below; referenced as applying a looser state-action standard)
Lugar v. Edmondson Oil Co., 457 U.S. 922 (1982) (core state-action / "under color of law" framework under § 1983)
Brentwood Academy v. Tennessee Secondary School Athletic Ass’n, 531 U.S. 288 (2001) (state-action entwinement principles)
Manhattan Community Access Corp. v. Halleck, 587 U.S. 802 (2019) (limits on treating private actors/venues as state actors; public-forum doctrine backdrop)
Davison v. Randall, 912 F.3d 666 (4th Cir. 2019) (official’s Facebook page as state action/public forum; commonly cited in this doctrinal area)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Alito’s administrability/chilling-effect argument is the hardest point, and it pushes against any “mushy totality” test untethered to objective signals of official capacity. But Lugar’s attribution inquiry is conduct-specific: where the account is held out and functionally used as an ongoing channel for official school-board communications and constituent engagement, the decision to block critics is fairly attributable to the State because it is enabled by (and presented as) the officeholder’s authority, not merely private editorial discretion. Justice Barrett’s reliance on Brentwood usefully reinforces that we can look to function and presentation without deeming the platform a state actor (consistent with Halleck), and we can craft a narrow rule keyed to whether the official used (or purported to use) the account as an instrument of office when controlling access. On these facts, treating the blocking as private would invite evasion through labels while allowing viewpoint discrimination in what the official has made an official channel of governance.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Alito’s administrability and chilling-effect concern is serious, but it does not overcome the text of § 1983 and its original understanding: liability attaches when conduct is “made possible only because the wrongdoer is clothed with the authority of state law,” not merely because an official speaks about public issues. Chief Justice Roberts’s focus on objective indicia—whether the official held the account out and used it as an instrument of office for official announcements and constituent access—supplies the needed limiting principle and keeps genuinely personal accounts outside the First Amendment’s reach. Halleck strengthens, rather than weakens, that conclusion: we are not converting the platform into a state actor; we are assessing the officeholder’s use of official authority to control access to an official channel. Under Lugar (and consistent with Brentwood’s emphasis on attribution in context, as Justice Barrett notes), viewpoint-based blocking in that official channel is fairly attributable to the State.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s proposal to treat an account “held out” as an ongoing channel for constituent engagement as state action has intuitive appeal, but it remains too indeterminate under Lugar because it turns liability on malleable cues of presentation and mixed use rather than on whether the official actually exercised (or purported to exercise) governmental power in the challenged act of blocking. Justice Barrett’s invocation of Brentwood entwinement similarly risks collapsing the state-action boundary whenever an official speaks about public business on a privately controlled platform; the platform’s infrastructure and access mechanisms remain private, and the official’s block looks like private editorial control absent formal designation, use of state resources, or an exclusive/official notice function. Halleck, in my view, counsels against constitutionalizing access decisions in privately hosted spaces based on a “totality” that is difficult to administer and will chill officials’ ordinary participation. I would adhere to objective indicia tied to official authority—rather than “held out” impressions—to avoid overextending § 1983 into routine political communication.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Alito’s chilling-effect/administrability concern is real, but it doesn’t undermine a pragmatic Lugar inquiry focused on the specific challenged act—blocking—and whether it is fairly attributable to the State because the official used the account as an instrument of office. Chief Justice Roberts’s objective-indicia framing answers the overbreadth problem by tying state action to how the account is held out and used for official announcements and constituent engagement, not to mere discussion of public issues or mixed personal content. Halleck, as multiple colleagues note, is satisfied because we are not converting the platform into a state actor; we are regulating an officeholder’s exercise of governmental communicative authority when she controls access to an official channel. Justice Barrett’s Brentwood totality/entwinement point reinforces that this is a fact-sensitive attribution analysis that prevents easy evasion and, in real-world terms, protects dissenting and vulnerable constituents from being excluded from the primary access point the official herself created.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Alito’s administrability concern is the best point for petitioner, but I don’t think it genuinely undermines Lugar’s attribution inquiry because the test can be tied to objective function: whether the official used the account as an instrument of office for official announcements and constituent engagement and then controlled access in that official capacity. Chief Justice Roberts’s framing helps tighten the rule in a pragmatic, text-focused way—state action turns on the official’s exercise (or pretense) of governmental communicative authority, not on whether the account contains political speech or personal content. Halleck doesn’t change that analysis because we are not treating the platform as the state actor; we are evaluating the official’s own conduct under color of law in managing an official channel. Justice Barrett’s Brentwood totality/entwinement point supports (rather than expands) a workable, fact-specific limiting principle that leaves genuinely personal accounts outside § 1983.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Alito’s administrability and chilling-effect concern is serious, but it does not overcome § 1983’s “under color of” limitation as construed in Lugar—liability attaches only when the specific challenged act is made possible by the official’s claimed authority, not whenever an official speaks on a private platform. Chief Justice Roberts’s proposed objective framing—asking whether the account is held out and used as an instrument of office for official announcements and constituent engagement—supplies the limiting principle Alito says is missing, while avoiding any suggestion (for Halleck purposes) that the platform itself is a state actor. Justice Barrett’s Brentwood point reinforces that this is an attribution inquiry focused on function and presentation; that fact-sensitive approach narrows, rather than expands, the state-action category by excluding genuinely personal accounts even if they mention public issues. On these facts, viewpoint-based blocking from an account operating as an official communicative channel is fairly attributable to the State and thus actionable.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Alito’s administrability concern is serious: a malleable “held out” test could chill officials’ mixed-use speech and effectively constitutionalize private online activity, which Halleck cautions against. But Chief Justice Roberts’s framing supplies an objective limiting principle consistent with Lugar: the question is whether the specific act of blocking was “made possible” by the official’s use (or pretense) of governmental authority in operating an account as an ongoing channel for school-board communications and constituent engagement, not whether the official merely discussed public issues. Justice Barrett’s Brentwood totality/entwinement point reinforces that this attribution inquiry is functional and context-specific without deeming the platform a state actor; it captures these facts while leaving truly personal accounts outside § 1983. Alito’s proposed requirement of formal designation or exclusive notice channel is too narrow and would invite evasion by officials who, in practice, run the main public-facing conduit of their office through “personal” accounts.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Alito’s administrability concern is serious, but I do not think it justifies tying state action to formal labels or exclusive channels; § 1983’s “under color of” language, as Lugar frames it, reaches misuse of authority that is fairly attributable to the State even when the mechanism is privately owned. Chief Justice Roberts’s objective-indicia framing answers Alito’s chilling-effect point by focusing on whether the official held the account out and used it as an instrument of office for ongoing official announcements and constituent engagement, making the access-control decision an exercise (or at least pretense) of official authority rather than private editorial discretion. Brentwood’s totality/entwinement analysis supports that attribution is fact-bound, and Halleck is not violated because we are not converting the platform into a state actor; the state actor is the officeholder who curated an official communicative channel and then excluded critics based on viewpoint. On these facts, treating the blocking decision as under color of law best fits the text, original public meaning, and our precedent without sweeping in genuinely personal accounts.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Alito’s administrability/chilling-effect concern is the petitioner’s strongest point, but I don’t think it undermines attribution here because Lugar asks whether the specific challenged act—blocking critics—was fairly attributable to the State, not whether the account ever mixed personal and public speech. Chief Justice Roberts’s emphasis on objective indicia that the page was held out and used as an ongoing channel for school-board communications and constituent engagement supplies a workable limiting principle that avoids constitutionalizing “ordinary participation” while preventing easy evasion by relabeling official channels as personal. Justice Barrett’s Brentwood totality/entwinement framing reinforces my pragmatic view that we should assess function and presentation in context rather than demand formal designation or exclusive use, which would be underinclusive and invite procedural unfairness in access to an official forum. Halleck remains satisfied because the platform is not deemed the state actor; the constitutional constraint attaches only when the officeholder uses the account as an instrument of governance and then excludes speakers based on viewpoint.

John Roberts.reasoning: Under § 1983, the “under color of law” and Fourteenth Amendment state-action inquiries typically converge. Lugar v. Edmondson Oil Co., 457 U.S. 922, 935 n.18, 937 (1982). When elected officials use an account as an extension of their office—regularly communicating about school-board business and inviting constituent engagement—the interactive space is fairly attributable to the State, and exclusion of critics is governmental conduct subject to the First Amendment. Consistent with Halleck’s insistence that state action turns on whether the challenged conduct is governmental rather than merely private, 587 U.S. 802 (2019), I would resolve this case narrowly: state action exists only where the official (on these facts) used the account to exercise or purport to exercise official authority in managing constituent access to official communications.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Under Lugar v. Edmondson Oil Co., § 1983 requires that the challenged conduct be “fairly attributable to the State,” and conduct that meets the constitutional state-action requirement also satisfies the statutory “under color of” requirement. Where an official uses a social-media account as an instrument of office—inviting constituent engagement on official business and communicating governmental information—the official’s control of access to the interactive features is an exercise (or misuse) of governmental authority, not merely private editorial discretion. Blocking constituents because of their views in that circumstance is state action and triggers First Amendment constraints, consistent with the limits on extending constitutional obligations to truly private hosts recognized in Manhattan Community Access Corp. v. Halleck. On these facts, the account’s official use supplies the close nexus required by Lugar, making the blocking attributable to the State.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 1983 reaches only conduct taken “under color of” state law, which is functionally equivalent to the Fourteenth Amendment’s state-action requirement, and thus demands that the challenged blocking be “fairly attributable to the State.” Lugar v. Edmondson Oil Co., 457 U.S. 922, 936 (1982). A public official does not act under color of law merely by speaking about public issues on a privately controlled social-media account; absent use of governmental authority or an account held out as an official channel, the moderation decision is best treated as private conduct, consistent with the limits on converting private property/choices into state action emphasized in Manhattan Community Access Corp. v. Halleck, 587 U.S. 802 (2019). A looser standard (like the Ninth Circuit’s) risks constitutionalizing vast amounts of officials’ mixed-use online activity and chilling ordinary, personal participation in public debate—practical consequences the state-action doctrine is designed to avoid. On these facts, the First Amendment should not be extended to compel access to interactive features of an account that is not clearly operated as an official governmental instrumentality.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Under Lugar v. Edmondson Oil Co., the § 1983 “under color of law” and constitutional state-action inquiries generally converge on whether the challenged conduct is “fairly attributable to the State,” 457 U.S. 922, 935 n.18, 937 (1982). When elected officials hold out a social-media page as an extension of their office—using it to communicate about school-board business and to solicit constituent engagement—the interactive features function as a channel of official governance, making viewpoint-based blocking action under color of law. Consistent with Davison v. Randall, 912 F.3d 666 (4th Cir. 2019), the officials’ purposeful use of the page for official communication supports treating the comment threads as at least a limited public forum for discussion of official matters, where the First Amendment forbids viewpoint discrimination. A narrower rule would invite evasion and would disproportionately burden constituents—especially vulnerable or dissenting voices—who increasingly rely on these channels for access to public officials and participation in civic life.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Under Lugar v. Edmondson Oil Co., the “under color of” and state-action inquiries generally track whether the challenged conduct is “fairly attributable to the State,” and here the officials’ blocking decisions were intertwined with their exercise of official authority over a channel they used for school-board communication and constituent engagement. Where an elected official holds an account out as an extension of office—using it to disseminate official information and solicit public feedback—the interactive space functions as a governmental communicative forum, and viewpoint-based exclusion triggers First Amendment constraints. That conclusion is consistent with Davison v. Randall’s treatment of an official’s social-media page as state action when used for official business, and it avoids the unworkable alternative of letting officials constitutionalize (or deconstitutionalize) moderation based solely on labeling an account “personal.” Halleck cautions against converting private platforms into state actors, but the relevant state actor here is the official, and the question is whether she used governmental authority in managing access—on these facts, she did.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 1983 reaches only conduct taken “under color of” state law, which tracks the state-action inquiry requiring the challenged conduct be “fairly attributable to the State.” Lugar v. Edmondson Oil Co., 457 U.S. 922, 936–37 (1982). When an official uses a social-media account as an instrument of office—holding it out as a channel for official announcements and constituent engagement about government business—the official is exercising authority made possible only by the office, and viewpoint-based blocking in that official channel is properly treated as state action subject to the First Amendment. This approach respects the separation between an official’s private speech and official conduct by asking whether the moderation decision is tied to the official’s governmental authority and duties, consistent with Halleck’s insistence that the First Amendment constrains governmental actors, not private ones. Manhattan Cmty. Access Corp. v. Halleck, 587 U.S. 802, 807–08 (2019).

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Under Lugar v. Edmondson Oil Co., 457 U.S. 922 (1982), conduct is actionable under § 1983 when it is fairly attributable to the State, including when an official invokes or exercises governmental authority rather than acting as a private citizen. Here, the officials used the pages as ongoing channels for official communication and constituent engagement about school-board business, so the interactive features functioned as an instrumentality of their office; blocking constituents in that setting is best understood as action “under color of” state law. Consistent with this Court’s forum cases, once an official intentionally opens a channel for discussion of official matters, viewpoint-based exclusions are constitutionally suspect even if the page originated as a campaign or mixed-use account. A narrower rule would invite evasions and prove unworkable in practice, undermining predictable First Amendment constraints on officials’ communications with the public.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Section 1983’s “under color of” requirement tracks the state-action inquiry, which turns on whether the challenged conduct is “fairly attributable to the State.” Lugar v. Edmondson Oil Co., 457 U.S. 922, 935–937 (1982). When an official uses an account as an instrument of office—holding it out as a channel for official announcements and constituent engagement—the official’s moderation of the interactive space is plausibly an exercise of authority “made possible only because the wrongdoer is clothed with the authority of state law,” and thus is attributable to the State for First Amendment purposes. That conclusion is consistent with Brentwood Academy’s totality-of-circumstances approach to attribution, 531 U.S. 288, 295 (2001), and with the warning in Halleck that private platforms are not themselves state actors, 587 U.S. 802 (2019), because the relevant actor here is the official exercising governmental communicative authority rather than the platform. On these facts, blocking critics in a space intentionally opened for discussion of official business constitutes state action and triggers the First Amendment’s limits on viewpoint discrimination.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Under § 1983, the relevant inquiry is whether the challenged exclusion is "fairly attributable to the State," and Lugar v. Edmondson Oil Co. makes clear that “under color of” law and Fourteenth Amendment state action typically rise or fall together. Where officials hold out a social-media page as an instrument of their office—using it to communicate school-board business and solicit constituent input—the interactive space functions as a channel of official engagement, and blocking critics is conduct enabled by and entwined with their governmental role rather than purely private moderation (cf. Brentwood Academy’s entwinement principles). Treating such exclusion as state action better vindicates procedural fairness by preventing viewpoint-based barriers to constituent participation in a forum the officials intentionally opened for official matters, while still leaving room to treat genuinely personal accounts as private under Manhattan Community Access Corp. v. Halleck. Because respondents plausibly allege state action/under-color-of-law and viewpoint discrimination in an official forum, I would affirm the judgment for respondents.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether an elected local official acts under color of state law (i.e., engages in state action) when they block constituents from interacting with the official’s social-media account that mixes personal content with information about official business.
case_analysis.legal_provision: U.S. Const. amend. I (free speech) and amend. XIV (state action requirement as applied to local officials), enforced via 42 U.S.C. § 1983 ("under color of" state law).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners (school-board members) argue that blocking the Garniers from their social-media pages was not "state action" / not "under color of" law because the accounts were personal or campaign-adjacent tools they controlled as private speakers, not government-controlled channels. They contend the Ninth Circuit applied an overly broad ("looser") test that effectively constitutionalizes ordinary moderation decisions by officials on mixed-use accounts, creating a circuit split with the Sixth Circuit’s more demanding approach (as reflected in Lindke v. Freed). They also point to practical administrability concerns for public officials who use social media and to the idea that, even if they sometimes posted about government, that does not convert the entire account into an official government forum.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents (the Garniers) argue the officials’ pages functioned as official communication tools—used to share information about board business, engage constituents, and convey matters tied to the officials’ public roles—so blocking critics is governmental censorship in a space that operates like a public forum (or at least a speech channel the officials used in their governmental capacities). They emphasize that the relevant inquiry is functional: whether the official used the account to perform or appear to perform official duties and to invite public interaction about governance. On that view, the officials’ decision to block based on viewpoint triggers First Amendment scrutiny and supports liability under § 1983.
key_precedents: Lindke v. Freed (Sixth Circuit; referenced as applying a more stringent state-action test)
Biden v. Knight First Amendment Institute, 141 S. Ct. 1220 (2021)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s and Justice Kagan’s anti-evasion point is the strongest case for Respondent, but it cannot substitute for § 1983’s requirement that the specific deprivation—the act of blocking—be fairly attributable to an actual or purported exercise of state-conferred authority, not merely to the account’s role as a convenient constituent forum. Justice Barrett and Justice Gorsuch argue that the relevant “power” is the office-linked, purported authority to transact with constituents in that space, yet under West v. Atkins and Classic the inquiry still must identify a misuse of governmental authority tied to the challenged act; otherwise we risk collapsing “under color” into “official-looking use,” an approach Halleck warns against by insisting on clear attribution principles. Lindke v. Freed, as Justice Kavanaugh emphasizes, points to a narrower, function-specific test, and I would reverse the Ninth Circuit’s totality approach and remand for application of that administrable standard rather than resolving state action on this record. I therefore remain with Petitioner, though I would write narrowly to avoid creating an evasion safe harbor and to clarify what evidence would satisfy Lindke on remand.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s anti-evasion concern is the strongest point for Respondent, but it cannot substitute for § 1983’s textual requirement that the challenged deprivation be “under color of” state law—i.e., traceable to power possessed by virtue of state law, not merely to an account’s practical importance or an official’s self-presentation. Justice Kagan and Justice Barrett recast the relevant “power” as the office-backed capacity to communicate with constituents in that space, but that risks collapsing the Classic/West v. Atkins inquiry into a “mantle of office” test untethered to any concrete exercise or purported exercise of official authority through the specific act of blocking. Lindke v. Freed, as the Chief Justice and Justice Kavanaugh emphasize, properly demands a function-specific nexus to the challenged act; on this record the blocking appears to be an exercise of private account control provided by a private platform, and Halleck (as Justice Gorsuch notes) reinforces the need to keep that state-action boundary disciplined. I would reverse the Ninth Circuit’s broader totality approach and remand for application of Lindke’s narrower duty/authority inquiry without diluting the statute’s attribution requirement.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s and Justice Sotomayor’s anti-evasion point is the strongest on the other side, but it cannot supply the missing statutory element: § 1983 requires that the challenged act (blocking) be undertaken through actual or purported authority “possessed by virtue of state law,” not merely through the practical importance of the forum. Their reframing of “power” as an official’s asserted capacity to speak “as the government” in that space risks collapsing the Classic/West inquiry into a test of prominence and presentation—precisely what Chief Justice Roberts warns would constitutionalize mixed personal accounts and chill officials’ own private speech. Lindke’s function-specific duty/authority framework, which Justice Barrett says still yields state action here, cuts the other way absent evidence that the access-control decision itself was made as an instrument of official duty rather than by virtue of private account control; Halleck reinforces our obligation to police that attribution line carefully. Because the record (as described) does not show the blocking was tied to any state-conferred authority beyond the official’s general “mantle of office,” I remain for reversal and remand under a narrower, act-focused standard.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh press the strongest point—§ 1983 demands a function-specific nexus between the challenged act (blocking) and actual or purported official authority, not a mere “official-looking” totality test—and I agree the Ninth Circuit’s broader language should be narrowed. But that narrowing does not change the outcome here because, as Justice Kagan explains, the record shows the interactive space was being used and held out as a constituent-facing channel for government business at the time of the blocks, so excluding critics was a misuse of office-backed authority to structure access to that official channel rather than private curation. Justice Thomas’s West v. Atkins/Classic framing does not require a discrete state-law “power to block”; it asks whether the defendant’s conduct was made possible and meaningful by virtue of office, and the “power” here is the asserted governmental capacity to receive and respond to constituents in that forum, with blocking functioning as the gatekeeping mechanism for that official communication stream. Halleck’s caution (raised by Justice Gorsuch) is satisfied because we are not converting the platform into a state actor; we are attributing the official’s exclusion decision to the State only when it operates as part of an official communications apparatus, a rule that is both administrable under Lindke and prevents easy evasion that predictably harms constituents with the least access to alternative channels.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s and Justice Kavanaugh’s strongest point—Lindke’s function-specific, act-tied inquiry—does not require reversal here; it supports affirmance because the record shows the account’s interactive space was being used and presented as an ongoing constituent-facing instrument for official communication when the blocking occurred. Justice Thomas’s West v. Atkins/Classic framing does not demand a discrete state-law “power to block”; it asks whether the defendant misused authority made meaningful by state law, and the exclusionary control here operated as part of the office-linked channel through which constituents were invited to engage the official. Justice Gorsuch’s Halleck caution is satisfied because we are not treating the platform as the State; we are attributing only the official’s access-control decision to the State when deployed in the course (or claimed course) of official business. I agree with Chief Justice Roberts that the Ninth Circuit’s totality language should be narrowed, but under that narrower, administrable standard the challenged blocking remains fairly attributable to the State on these facts.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kavanaugh’s best point is administrability: § 1983 cannot hinge on a freewheeling “official-looking” or mixed-use totality test, and Lindke rightly demands a function-specific inquiry tied to the challenged act. But applying that narrower Lindke frame, the blocking here is fairly attributable to the State because—on this record—the account was being used and held out as an ongoing constituent-facing channel for governance communications when the exclusion occurred, so the access control functioned as an instrument (or purported instrument) of official duty rather than merely private curation. Justice Thomas’s insistence on a discrete state-law “authority to block” is too cramped under Classic and West v. Atkins: § 1983 reaches misuse of authority made meaningful by office, and the relevant state-conferred authority is the official’s claimed capacity to transact with constituents as the government in that space, not a statutory power to click a platform button. Halleck reinforces the need for disciplined attribution, but once the challenged conduct is identified as an office-linked act of exclusion from an official channel, Halleck does not defeat state action—it cautions only against treating the platform itself as the State.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Sotomayor rightly stress anti-evasion: officials should not be able to run constituent-facing governance through a nominally personal page and dodge the First Amendment. But that concern cannot supply § 1983’s “under color of” element without collapsing it into an “official-looking” or “important channel” test; as the Chief Justice explains, Lindke v. Freed is the administrable way to address evasion by demanding a tight, act-specific showing that the blocking itself was done pursuant to (or in purported exercise of) official authority, not merely alongside official communications. I do not read West v. Atkins and Classic to treat the generalized “mantle of office” in an online space as the relevant state-conferred power, and I agree with Justice Thomas that we should not dilute the state-action boundary simply because the platform tool is influential or the account is mixed-use. The proper course is to reverse the Ninth Circuit’s totality approach and remand for application of Lindke’s function-specific inquiry to the blocking decision on this record.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The strongest point from the Petitioners—pressed by Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh—is administrability: we cannot let “mixed-use” or “official-looking” content alone satisfy § 1983, and Lindke properly demands a tight, act-specific nexus. But applying Lindke’s duty/authority framework as Roberts frames it, the blocking here is still fairly attributable to the State because (as Justice Kagan emphasizes) the account was being used and held out as an ongoing instrument for constituent-facing governance communication when the exclusion occurred, making the access control part of the purported exercise of office authority. Justice Thomas’s insistence on a discrete state-law “power to block” reads Classic and West too narrowly; those cases ask whether the defendant misused authority made meaningful by virtue of state law, not whether state law specifically conferred the platform’s technical feature. I would, however, narrow the Ninth Circuit’s totality language in line with the Chief Justice to avoid collapsing the inquiry into mere “official-ish” presentation, while concluding the record still meets the under-color requirement on these facts.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s administrability concern is the best point for Petitioner, but I don’t think his “blocking tool is private account control” framing (echoed by Justice Kavanaugh) answers the Lindke question on this record: the account’s interactive space was being used and held out as an ongoing constituent-facing channel for governance, and the blocking thus functioned as an exclusion from participation in that office-linked forum. Justice Thomas’s reliance on Classic and West v. Atkins does not require a discrete state-law power to click “block”; it requires that the deprivation be accomplished through authority made meaningful by virtue of state law, and here the official’s asserted capacity to conduct constituent business in that space supplies the necessary nexus. Halleck (as Justice Gorsuch notes) counsels discipline in attribution and cautions against converting the platform into the State, but attributing the official’s access-control decision to the State—when used as an instrument of official communication—does not do that. I would still narrow the Ninth Circuit’s totality language as Roberts suggests, yet under a function-specific duty/authority test the outcome remains state action here.

John Roberts.reasoning: Liability under 42 U.S.C. § 1983 requires that the challenged act be taken “under color of” state law, which in turn demands a sufficiently close connection between the blocking decision and the official’s actual governmental authority under the Fourteenth Amendment state-action requirement. A mixed-use account’s “official-looking” content or discussion of public business, standing alone, is an administrable but overbroad basis to constitutionalize ordinary moderation choices and risks sweeping private speech by officials-as-citizens into First Amendment forum doctrine. Consistent with the more demanding approach reflected in Lindke v. Freed, the better—and narrower—rule is that state action exists only when the official uses the account as a channel for performing (or purporting to perform) an official duty with authority derived from office, not merely because the account references governmental matters. On this record, the Ninth Circuit’s totality test is too loose; I would reverse and remand for application of a tighter “actual authority/official use” standard tied to the specific act of blocking.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Section 1983’s text reaches only deprivations committed “under color of any statute, ordinance, regulation, custom, or usage, of any State,” which this Court has long understood to require an exercise or misuse of power “possessed by virtue of state law.” West v. Atkins, 487 U.S. 42, 49 (1988) (quoting United States v. Classic, 313 U.S. 299, 326 (1941)). Blocking users from a privately controlled social-media account—even one that intermittently discusses official business—does not itself invoke any state-conferred authority or statutory power, and the First and Fourteenth Amendments do not convert an official’s private speech platform into a state forum absent a showing that the official was performing an actual or apparent duty of office through that channel. The Ninth Circuit’s functional approach risks untethering “under color of” law from any identifiable state authority and expanding § 1983 beyond its textual limits, effectively federalizing ordinary online moderation by officeholders.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 1983 requires action taken “under color of” state law, and that boundary is not satisfied merely because an official sometimes discusses government matters on a privately controlled, mixed-use social-media account. Consistent with Lindke v. Freed’s emphasis on whether the challenged conduct is cloaked with official authority (and the administrable need to distinguish private speech from governmental action), a court should require a concrete showing that the official used governmental power or purported to exercise official duties in operating the interactive features at issue, not simply that the account contained some official information. A post-by-post or function-specific approach to mixed-use accounts avoids constitutionalizing ordinary moderation decisions and respects officials’ own First Amendment interests while keeping truly official channels within the First Amendment’s constraints. Because the Ninth Circuit’s broader test risks converting personal platforms into state fora whenever an official mixes in public business, I would reverse and find no state action on these facts absent stronger indicia of official control or authority under § 1983 and the Fourteenth Amendment.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Under 42 U.S.C. § 1983 and the Fourteenth Amendment’s state-action requirement, an elected official acts “under color of” law when she uses a social-media account as a functional channel for performing (or purporting to perform) official duties—announcing government business, soliciting constituent input, and leveraging the authority of office—then excludes critics based on viewpoint. Even under the Sixth Circuit’s framing in Lindke v. Freed, the dispositive inquiry is whether the official is exercising actual or purported governmental authority in operating the interactive space; when the account is used to communicate and administer public-facing aspects of the job, blocking constituents is not private moderation but governmental censorship. Treating such mixed-use accounts as beyond constitutional scrutiny would allow officials to evade the First Amendment by relocating core public communication to privately controlled platforms, disproportionately harming vulnerable speakers who rely on accessible online forums to petition and criticize government. Biden v. Knight First Amendment Institute underscores that when an official uses social media as an instrument of governance, the interactive features function like a public-facing forum where viewpoint-based exclusion triggers First Amendment constraints.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Under 42 U.S.C. § 1983, the question is whether the officials exercised (or purported to exercise) actual authority of their offices when operating the interactive portions of these mixed-use accounts, not whether the accounts contained some personal material. Where an elected official uses a page to announce board business, solicit and respond to constituent input about governance, and presents the page as an extension of official duties, blocking critics functions as an exercise of governmental power and is therefore action “under color of” state law for First and Fourteenth Amendment purposes. That approach aligns with the functional, authority-based framework this Court articulated for mixed-use social-media accounts in Lindke v. Freed and avoids the administrability problems of treating an entire account as purely private despite sustained official use. Biden v. Knight First Amendment Institute underscores that the constitutional analysis turns on the official’s use of governmental authority to control an interactive space for public discussion, even though it did not reach the merits.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 1983 applies only when a defendant acts “under color of any statute, ordinance, regulation, custom, or usage” of a State, and our cases treat that inquiry as equivalent to the Fourteenth Amendment’s state-action requirement. See 42 U.S.C. § 1983; West v. Atkins, 487 U.S. 42, 49 (1988). When an elected official uses an account as an instrument to perform (and to appear to perform) official duties—announcing board business, soliciting constituent input, and communicating in their governmental capacity—the official’s control over access and interaction derives from the authority of office, not merely private choice, and viewpoint-based blocking in that channel is governmental censorship subject to the First Amendment. Cf. Manhattan Cmty. Access Corp. v. Halleck, 139 S. Ct. 1921, 1928 (2019) (First Amendment constrains governmental, not private, abridgment). On these facts, the mixed personal content does not defeat state action where the challenged conduct is tied to the official use of the account to carry out public responsibilities.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Section 1983 imposes liability only for conduct taken “under color of” state law, and the First and Fourteenth Amendments therefore require a careful, workable line between an official’s private speech and attributable government action. Under Lindke v. Freed, a public official’s social-media moderation is state action only when the official exercises actual (or purported) governmental authority or performs actual official duties through the account; mixed-use posting about public issues alone does not convert the entire page into a governmental forum. The Ninth Circuit’s more expansive approach risks constitutionalizing routine, practical moderation choices by officials on personal or campaign-adjacent accounts, undermining administrability and chilling officials’ own protected speech. On this record, absent a clearer showing that the blocking was done pursuant to official authority or duties—rather than personal control of a private account—the conduct is not fairly attributable to the State for § 1983 purposes.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Section 1983 reaches only conduct taken “under color of” state law, which in original public meaning and this Court’s state-action cases turns on whether the official exercised (or purported to exercise) governmental authority rather than acting as a private citizen. Where an elected official uses a social-media account as an ongoing channel for carrying out the work of office—announcing official actions, inviting constituent input on governance, and presenting the page as an extension of the official role—blocking constituents from that interactive space is fairly attributable to the State and thus constitutes state action under the Fourteenth Amendment and § 1983. That conclusion is consistent with the functional inquiry suggested by this Court’s disposition in Biden v. Knight First Amendment Institute, which recognized that an official’s use of a private platform can nonetheless present serious First Amendment concerns when used for official communication. On these facts, the account’s mixed personal content does not defeat state action where the challenged act (blocking constituents from official-facing interactions) is tied to the performance and appearance of official duties.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Under § 1983 and the Fourteenth Amendment’s state-action requirement, an elected official acts “under color of” law when exercising authority made possible by the office and using an account as a functional channel for official communication and constituent engagement. Where an account mixes personal posts with regular dissemination of government information and invites the public to interact about official business, blocking constituents because of their criticism is best understood as governmental conduct with concrete, exclusionary consequences for participation in local governance, triggering First Amendment constraints. Biden v. Knight First Amendment Institute underscores that an official’s use of social media for public-facing governance can implicate First Amendment limits even on privately owned platforms, and the “duty/authority” focus (as framed in Lindke v. Freed) supports treating account management as state action when tied to the official’s role rather than purely private speech. Procedural fairness and practical consequences favor a rule that prevents viewpoint-based exclusion from an official-facing channel that the official has effectively held out as a venue for public business.
